paper_a.title: Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data

metadata.description: Paper A (FedAvg, McMahan et al. 2017) extends paper B's (Zinkevich et al. 2010) one-shot 'partition + local SGD + average' template (SimuParallelSGD / ParallelSGD) to the federated setting: (i) iterates the local-SGD-then-average step over many communication rounds, (ii) drops paper B's IID/convex assumptions in favor of explicitly non-IID, unbalanced, massively distributed clients on non-convex deep networks, and (iii) adds client subsampling, per-client epoch/batch hyperparameters, and weighted aggregation. Paper B is cited in paper A as the prior baseline (one-shot model averaging). This is a clear EXT relationship: same algorithmic primitive (local SGD + parameter averaging), reframed and broadened for federated learning.

matches.explanation: Both papers state the same finite-sum risk-minimization template min_w (1/n) sum_i f_i(w). Paper B fixes the per-example loss to a regularized convex form c^i(w) = (lambda/2)||w||^2 + L(x^i,y^i,w.x^i) and assumes IID data; paper A generalizes the same finite sum to a partition across K clients with weights n_k/n, drops convexity/IID, and adds the communication-budget constraint. Same problem schema, broader assumptions in A — analogous rather than exact.

Paper A's local objective F_k(w) = (1/n_k) sum_{i in P_k} f_i(w) is the per-client analogue of paper B's overall risk c(w) = (1/m) sum_i c^i(w). The structural role is identical (average loss over a fixed example set), but A indexes one such object per client to expose the partition, while B has a single global one. The per-example f_i / c^i correspondence is implicit.

Paper A formalizes the client data partition {P_k} as a first-class definition (with possibly unbalanced n_k and arbitrary non-IID structure), whereas paper B introduces partitioning only inside SimuParallelSGD as a uniform-size random split (T = floor(m/k) examples per machine). Same conceptual object — a partition of the training set across workers — but A treats it as part of the problem and B treats it as an algorithm step. Cross-type (definition vs algorithm_step) match is justified because the partition itself is the shared concept.

The IID-vs-non-IID definition is paper A's central contribution to framing. Paper B implicitly assumes IID partitioning (uniform random split) and never names or studies the non-IID regime, so there is no counterpart.

Paper A's definition of the federated optimization setting (non-IID, unbalanced, massively distributed, communication-limited) has no analogue in paper B, whose setup is data-center MapReduce-style parallelism with IID, balanced shards and no communication budget. This is a paper-A-original conceptual contribution.

The notion of federated learning itself (clients hold private data, only updates are shared, central server coordinates) does not appear in paper B, which is framed entirely as data-center parallelization. Paper-A-original definition.

The expected-local-updates-per-round parameter u = nE/(KB) is specific to FedAvg's iterated-rounds protocol with local epochs E and minibatch size B; paper B's single-pass SimuParallelSGD has no equivalent (it has only T = m/k local steps and no notion of repeated rounds).
MNIST pathological non-IID partition is a paper-A-original empirical construction for stress-testing non-IID FedAvg; no counterpart in paper B (no MNIST experiments, no non-IID experiments).
Shakespeare per-role client dataset is a paper-A-original benchmark construction. Paper B uses only an industrial email dataset with no per-user partitioning.

Paper A's FedSGD baseline (one synchronous round = each client computes one full-batch gradient, server aggregates by weighted average) is the iterated-rounds version of paper B's ParallelSGD (run independent SGDs on k machines, then average once). EP307.1 is the gradient-aggregation form, EP307.2 is the equivalent model-averaging form — both reduce to ParallelSGD's averaging primitive when run for one round with one local step. Paper A explicitly cites paper B's lineage (Zinkevich et al. 2010) as a precursor.

FedAvg (paper A) is the multi-round, client-subsampled, non-IID-tolerant generalization of SimuParallelSGD (paper B). Both algorithms instantiate the same primitive: (a) local SGD on each worker over its data shard, (b) parameter averaging on a server. SimuParallelSGD does this once over a uniform partition with no client sampling; FedAvg iterates it over T communication rounds, samples a C-fraction of K clients per round, runs E local epochs with minibatches of size B, and uses weighted averaging by n_k. Paper A's algorithm reduces to a single-round version of paper B's when E=1, B=full-batch, C=1, and partition is IID/balanced. EP307.3 is the iterated local-update primitive that distinguishes FedAvg from FedSGD/ParallelSGD.

Composite L2 alignment of the two algorithms' step DAGs (parent L1 match emitted above). Step-by-step: A's initialize-global-model (ASP307.1) maps to B's local-init w_{i,0}=0 + partition (ASP308.1+ASP308.2); A adds a sample-client-subset step (ASP307.2) with no B counterpart (B uses all k machines every run); A's parallel-ClientUpdate dispatch (ASP307.3) plus the inner local-minibatch-SGD loop (ASP307.5) correspond to B's local-SGD loop (ASP308.3); A's weighted aggregation (ASP307.4) corresponds to B's uniform 1/k averaging (ASP308.4). Key differences: A iterates the whole sequence over T rounds and uses weighted averaging by n_k; B runs the whole pipeline once with uniform weights.

Paper A explicitly cites 'Zinkevich et al. 2010' (paper B) as one of the references for one-shot model averaging (AP307.3 is paper A's external description of paper B's algorithm). This is a paper-A-external <-> paper-B-paper origin match: the cited result IS paper B's SimuParallelSGD. The cited claim that 'in the worst case (convex, IID setting), the resulting global model is no better than a model trained on a single client' is paper A's restatement of paper B's worst-case discussion.
Asynchronous parameter-server SGD (Dean et al. 2012) is cited only in paper A. Paper B's MapReduce / synchronous-averaging framework is precisely the alternative to async PS SGD.

Iterative local-model averaging (McDonald 2010, Povey 2015, elastic averaging 2015) is cited in paper A as related prior work on iterated averaging. None of these specific citations appear in paper B (which predates Povey 2015 and elastic averaging and cites a different prior-work set in its Section 1).
MNIST 2NN is paper-A-original empirical; no MNIST experiment in paper B.
MNIST CNN is paper-A-original empirical; paper B uses only convex linear models (no CNN).
Shakespeare LSTM is paper-A-original empirical; no language modeling in paper B.
CIFAR-10 CNN experiment is paper-A-original empirical; no analogue in paper B.

Both papers include a single 'real-world large-scale' empirical study on a proprietary text-like corpus, demonstrating wall-clock or round-count speedup from their parallel/federated optimizer (paper A: 23x fewer rounds for word-LSTM on social posts; paper B: linear scalability of SimuParallelSGD on email Huber/squared-loss training). The matching is conceptual (large-scale validation example), not by content — different model class (LSTM vs convex linear) and different metric (rounds vs wall-clock); marked low-confidence.

Figure-1 averaging illustration (shared init makes parameter averaging work on non-convex deep nets) is paper-A-original empirical; paper B's analysis is purely convex and does not address the non-convex shared-init phenomenon.

The 'communication is dominant cost, trade compute for rounds' design principle is paper-A-original framing; paper B's setting (data-center MapReduce) treats communication and computation as comparable and aims for wall-clock speedup, not round reduction.
Erratum on aggregation weights (sum over sampled set S_t, not all K) is paper-A-specific. Paper B has no client subsampling, so the issue does not arise.
The implicit-regularization-of-model-averaging conjecture is paper-A-original (motivated by deep-net experiments); paper B's convex analysis has no such phenomenon.
The 'decay E in late training' heuristic for FedAvg is paper-A-specific; paper B has no E parameter (single pass per machine).
Privacy-via-data-processing-inequality remark is paper-A-original framing; privacy is not discussed in paper B.
DP/SMPC-secure FedAvg is paper-A-original future work; paper B has no privacy or DP discussion.

Paper A explicitly leaves convergence theory for FedAvg open (especially non-convex, non-IID). Paper B *answers* the analogous open question for the IID convex case via Theorem 12 (main bound for ParallelSGD), supported by Theorems 8/9/10 (Wasserstein contraction of SGD operator + bias and variance of stationary distribution). This is a paper-A-paper-origin <-> paper-B-paper-origin alignment between an open problem and the prior result that partially resolves its convex/IID restriction — direct evidence that paper A is an EXT of paper B.

Paper B's SGD update map phi^i(w) = w - eta nabla c^i(w) (a single-step view used in the contraction analysis) has no L1 counterpart in paper A; paper A treats SGD updates only operationally inside ClientUpdate.
Critical learning rate eta* (the largest eta making the SGD step a contraction) is paper-B-specific; paper A treats eta as a tuned hyperparameter without a contraction-based bound.
Lifted distribution map p (pushforward of phi on parameter distributions) is paper-B-original; paper A does not analyze the parameter distribution.
Mixture SGD operator p* and parameter distribution D_eta^t are paper-B-original constructs for the Wasserstein-contraction analysis.
Holder seminorm definition is a paper-B-original technical tool used in the higher-order Kantorovich-Rubinstein extension; no counterpart in paper A.
Relative standard deviation sigma_X^c is a technical paper-B definition for the variance-of-an-i.i.d.-average lemma; no counterpart in paper A.
Lipschitz-bounded loss gradient is paper-B's analytic assumption for the contraction proofs. Paper A makes no formal assumption on losses (no convergence theory).

Paper B's plain single-machine SGD is the inner routine of ParallelSGD/SimuParallelSGD. Paper A's local minibatch SGD inside ClientUpdate plays the same role but is described only as an algorithm step (ASP307.5), already aligned in the composite L2 entry. No standalone L1 SGD algorithm in paper A.
Lemma 3 (SGD step is a contraction with constant 1-eta lambda) is paper-B-original analysis; paper A has no contraction analysis.
Pointwise-contraction-lifts-to-Wasserstein lemma is a paper-B-original technical tool.
Mixture-of-contractions-is-a-contraction lemma is a paper-B-original technical tool.
Uniform contraction constant for mixtures (Corollary 7) is paper-B-original.
Theorem 8 (SGD operator is a Wasserstein contraction with stationary distribution) is paper-B-original. Paper A has no convergence theorem.
Theorem 9 (bias of stationary mean <= 2 eta G^2) is paper-B-original.
Theorem 10 (variance of stationary distribution = O(eta G^2/lambda)) is paper-B-original.
Theorem 11 (cost gap from a near-mean distribution via W_2) is paper-B-original technical bridge.

Theorem 12 (main convergence bound for ParallelSGD with k machines) is paper-B-original. This is the result paper A's open-problem entry OpenP307.2 conceptually points back to (already noted as analogous in that match).
Pairwise-contraction theorem (Theorem 17) is paper-B-original technical lemma.
Strongly-convex centering and contraction lemmas (Lemmas 14-16) are paper-B-original technical tools for the contraction analysis.
Higher-order Kantorovich-Rubinstein extension (Theorem 24) is paper-B-original.
Means closer than W_1 (Corollary 23) is paper-B-original.
Boundedness of SGD iterates (Theorem 44) is paper-B-original.
Closed-form Bellman solution (Theorem 65) and stationary E[w^2] bound (Theorem 66) are paper-B-original auxiliary MDP machinery.
Stochastic gradient update equation with L_2 regularization is paper-B-specific (regularized convex setting). Paper A has no analogous standalone equation.
Discussion of paper B's bound (wall-clock vs iteration tradeoffs) is paper-B-specific.

Comparison to prior parallel-SGD approaches (distributed subgradient, distributed convex solver, multicore SGD) is a paper-B-specific positioning remark referring to a different prior-work set than paper A's.
